newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks open depends on jobs data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks open depends on jobs data.

text.p: April employment data will set the stage for U.S. stocks and the bond market on Friday morning and help the guessing game over whether the Federal Reserve will continue to hike interest rates.

"The economy is coming along in a strong fashion and the question is does it need reigning in?" said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities. "The data will help us determine what the Fed will do on May 20 and whether there will be more tightening. It's a signpost by the road. The numbers are a big deal for the market."
The data are due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. According to a Reuter survey of U.S. economists, non-farm payrolls are expected to have risen to 211,000 in April from the previous month's 175,000.

The unemployment rate is forecast at an unchanged 5.2 percent. Average hourly earnings are expected up 0.3 percent compared with 0.4 percent in March and the Average workweek is expected to have fallen to 34.7 hours from 34.8 hours.
"Any wide variance -- a decline in the unemployment rate, a 50,000 increase in payrolls -- could influence the market to the downside," Wachtel said.

In Tokyo, stocks surged on Friday to close at a new high for 1997, lifted by institutional investors, mostly pension funds, seeking blue chip issues. The Nikkei Average rose 239.42 points, or 1.24 percent, to end at 19,514.75.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was up 11.4 at 4456.4.

U.S. shares were mixed with an overall firmer bias on Friday as the markets stayed quiet, awaiting the labor market data. Gainers included Intel Corp, up 1/4 at 154 and Philip Morris Cos Inc, up 1/4 at 39-1/4. Boeing Co shares were down 1/2 at 98-1/2.
The dollar was steady against the yen and drifted in Europe ahead of the payroll data.
U.S. Treasuries were mostly higher, with the long bond up 3/32 to yield 6.91 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that most on Wall Street believe that Nike Inc athletic shoes -- particularly its styles which sell for more than $100 -- are still hot among inner city kids and the suburban kids who imitate them. But analysts say that investors are worried anyway. Growth is definitely slowing, many Wall Streeters say.

The New York Times Market Place writes that the turmoil at Fidelity Investments moved up the corporate ladder yesterday as James C. Curvey was named chief operating officer and chairman of the company's operating committee.

This puts him in charge of day-to-day business and making him second in command to Fidelity's chairman, Edward C. Johnson 3rd. Industry analysts say the move makes clear that Johnson has grown weary of lingering doubts about the company's ability to continue dominating the mutual fund business.
